newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Rwandan Hutus near journey's end, questions remain.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan Hutus near journey's end, questions remain.
newsitem.dateline: MBANDAKA, Democratic Republic of the Congo 1997-06-24

text.p: For some, a makeshift graveyard near a former hospital in the tropical rain forest near the mighty Congo River is journey's end.
How they or other Rwandan Hutu refugees died is a question a U.N. massacre investigation will seek to answer, after receiving the go-ahead from Laurent Kabila's government in Kinshasa.
For the survivors, there's a flight home to Rwanda on a U.N. chartered plane -- and the end to a 2,000-km nightmare trek through the equatorial rainforest that cloaks Africa's third largest nation.

"It is time to go home now," says Ange Bagachugacha, 23, a former student and stronger looking new arrival in Mbandaka, a river port in the north west of Kabila's Congo and scene of an alleged massacre by his forces or their allies in May.
"I want to look for my family, and help to reconstruct my country," he adds.
He and others say fear of persecution -- some had a part in the 1994 genocide of up to a million ethnic Tutsis in Rwanda -- has been overtaken by a desire to end his journey.

A cargo plane left Mbandaka on Tuesday with around 300 refugees bound for Kigali. The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR has flown home 52,000 of the refugees in Kabila's Congo after the seven-month civil war, in over 2,000 rotations.
But they estimate up to 200,000 of the 1.2 million refugees who fled to the then Zaire in 1994 are still unaccounted for.
Rwandan Hutus still emerge in hundreds from the rainforest after fleeing fighting and attacks in the eastern border regions after the civil war began in October.
Over 100 arrived on a barge on Tuesday in Mbandaka port. At least 18 were seriously ill. Several children, little more than skin on their bones, looked unlikely to survive more than a day.

Mbandaka is the capital of ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko's Equateur province. It fell to Kabila's forces on May 13. Like most other towns in former Zaire, inhabitants say they longed for the change.
But allegations of massacres at the port and Wenge, a village 22 km into the forest, clouded their "liberation" from three decades of Mobutu rule.

"We have seen how they killed the refugees. Everybody in the town knows what happened," a young Congolese man said. He sheltered three escapees until they handed themselves in to the UNHCR on Tuesday.
A team of U.N. investigators who arrived in the capital Kinshasa on Friday is due to visit Mbandaka and numerous other alleged massacre sites.

The deputy governor, a native of the region who was in Mbandaka around the time of the alleged killings, says the team will be free to carry out their work. "There are a lot of rumours but they must provide some proof. I for one did not see any bodies," Edmond Mondombo told Reuters.
Local residents suggest some bodies were dumped in the Congo river. Local aid workers say they buried 113 bodies, which they estimate accounted for around a third of those killed.
